paragraphs.text: LIFE OF SAINT EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF CONSTANTIA IN CYPRUS. 1. Epiphanius was by birth a Phoenician, from the region around [?]

…his [?] how to bring up Epiphanius and his sister, since they lived in modest circumstances. They had a beast of burden for their work, but it was unruly. His mother said to Epiphanius, “Child, our household is in hard straits for our bodily needs and we are short of food. Take the animal we have at home, go to the fair and sell it, so that we can provide for our keep.” Epiphanius said to his mother, “Mother, you know that our animal is unruly. If I go to sell it, the men gathered there will know how unruly it is, and they will punish me, saying, ‘You had a bad thing, so by the law you shall suffer badly.’” His mother said, “Go, child. The God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will give the animal good sense, so that its price may provide for us.” So Epiphanius called on God, who gave Moses the grace to perform the greatest signs before Pharaoh, and set out, wishing to fulfil his obedience to his own mother. 2. And when he came to the fair, the unruly animal became well-behaved and full of gentleness. A Jewish merchant named Jacob came up and said to Epiphanius, “Boy, do you want to sell this animal?” Epiphanius said, “Yes, father; that is why I have brought it here.” Jacob said to Epiphanius, “What is your religion?” Epiphanius said, “I am a Jew.” Jacob said, “Since we are of the same people, child, let us not take sin as a go-between against ourselves. Rather, since we belong to a just God, let us set a just price for the animal, so that you are not wronged and I suffer no loss. Otherwise we may bring curses on ourselves afterwards and God will be angry with us; let it rather be blessings. For it is said, ‘Whoever blesses is blessed, and whoever curses is cursed.’” When Epiphanius heard this, he greatly feared Jacob's condemnation, and said to him, “I no longer want to sell you this animal.” Jacob said to Epiphanius, “For what reason, child?” Epiphanius said to him, “This animal, father, is unruly, and the hardship of a most bitter hunger has come upon my house. I have a mother and a sister, for my father has departed this human life. So my mother told me to sell the animal because we needed food. But now I have heard from you, father, that it is wicked to do harm, and I was afraid of God, lest you should curse me and God punish me through the curse laid on me.” 3. When Jacob heard this, he marvelled at the boy's answer. He took three gold coins and gave them to Epiphanius, instructing him with these words: “Child, take this gift and go to your mother, and you will bring bread into your

house. Take this animal back with you too. If it changes its bad and unruly disposition, let it stay in your house; but if it persists in its unruliness, drive it out of your house, lest it kill one of your family.” When Epiphanius heard this, he took the three gold coins from Jacob, took the animal, and set off for his village. About a mile along, a Christian named Cleobius met him and said to him, “Are you selling the animal, child?” Epiphanius answered, “No, father.” Cleobius said, “If you are selling it, take its price and let me have it.” While Cleobius was saying this to Epiphanius, the animal bolted wildly, fell upon Epiphanius, and flung him violently to the ground; and it went off the road. So Cleobius went on his way, and Epiphanius went into his village to his mother. When his mother saw him, she welcomed him joyfully, and he told her everything that had happened to him because of the unruly animal. Some time later Epiphanius's mother said to him, “Look, child, the land is neglected, and we get no support from it.” For they had a small piece of land of their own; his father had farmed it with great toil and drawn some support from it. So his mother said, “Let us sell our little plot to a farmer. And you go to some God-fearing man and be taught a trade, by which you can support yourself and provide bread for me and your sister.” 4. Now there was a Jewish teacher of the Law in Eleutheropolis, an admirable and devout man according to the Law of Moses. He owned property in the village where Epiphanius was born; he had known his father and was acquainted with his mother, and likewise with Epiphanius and his sister. Coming to inspect his property, he said to Epiphanius's mother, “Woman, will you give me your son as a son? Then you and your daughter will have your needs supplied from our house.”

When Epiphanius's mother heard this from the lawyer, she was overjoyed, and she took Epiphanius and handed him over to him at once as a son. The lawyer's name was Tryphon. He had an only daughter, and he wanted to marry her to Epiphanius. 5. So Tryphon took Epiphanius as his son and diligently taught him the Law and, with precision, the Hebrew letters. But Tryphon's daughter died, and Epiphanius alone remained in his house, growing both in stature and in Hebrew wisdom. Then Tryphon too happened to die, and he left all his estate to Epiphanius. Epiphanius's mother also died. Epiphanius took his sister into the house that Tryphon had left him, and the two lived together in the house in a very well-ordered way of life, according to Tryphon's teaching. Once, when Epiphanius went out to the village where he was born, where he also held the property Tryphon had left him, he was met by a Christian man named Lucian, an admirable and learned man who lived the solitary life. His trade was that of a calligrapher; he applied himself to it, earned his bread by it, and gave what was left over to the needy. Epiphanius was riding a beast of burden, while the blessed Lucian was walking along the road, and the two met. It happened that a poor man seized Lucian's feet and said to him, “Man of God, have mercy on me, for I have gone three days without food and have nothing at all.” The blessed Lucian, having nothing to give the poor man, took off his cloak and handed it over, saying, “Go into the city, sell this, and buy bread.” 6. Epiphanius noticed that as soon as Lucian had stripped himself and given his cloak to the poor man, he saw a white robe come down from heaven and cover him. Epiphanius was seized with great fear; throwing himself from his mount, he fell on his face and said to Lucian, “I beg you, sir, tell me: who are you?” The blessed Lucian said to Epiphanius, “You tell me what your religion is, and I will tell you about myself.” Epiphanius answered, “I am a Jew.” Then Lucian knew that the grace of God had come upon Epiphanius, for Lucian had the gift of foreknowledge. Lucian answered Epiphanius, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask a Christian to learn who I am? For Jews are an abomination to Christians, and Christians to Jews. There, you have heard that I am a Christian; you may not hear anything else from me.” Epiphanius said to Lucian, “And what prevents me too from becoming a Christian?” Lucian answered, “Unwillingness prevents it; for the willing is within reach.” Epiphanius was cut to the heart by Lucian's words; he no longer went on to inspect his property, but took Lucian and brought him to the house

that had been left to him, and showed him everything in his house, saying, “All this is mine, father. But I want to become a Christian and take up the solitary life. And this is my sister. What do you bid me do about these things?” The blessed Lucian said to Epiphanius, “Child, you cannot take up the solitary life while you have all these possessions. But give your sister in marriage to a husband and give her what she needs, and give the rest to those in need. Then you will be able to live well as a monk.” Epiphanius said to Lucian, “First, father, make me a Christian; then I will do everything you have instructed me.” Lucian said to Epiphanius, “I am not permitted to make you a Christian without the bishop.” 7. Having said this, Lucian left Epiphanius's house and went to the bishop. Epiphanius, without delay, said to his sister, “I want to become a Christian and take up the solitary life.” His sister said to him, “As you will, I will; as you do, I will do.” Lucian reported to the bishop about Epiphanius. The bishop said to Lucian, “Go and instruct him, and when we come into the church, have him prostrate himself before God, the lover of mankind.” So Lucian went to Epiphanius's house. When Epiphanius and his sister saw him, they fell on their faces and took hold of Lucian's feet, weeping and saying, “We beg you, father, make us become Christians.” So Lucian, drawing on the divine Scriptures, instructed them thoroughly. And they persisted in their entreaty, saying, “Make us become Christians.” So Lucian took the two of them together and went to the church. When the bishop came in, they fell on their faces and begged him to illuminate them. As the bishop entered the church, they followed behind with Lucian to hear the divine [?]

8. As Epiphanius drew near the outer doors of the church and stepped onto the first step of the building, the shoe fell off his left foot. When he had stepped up with his left foot and was about to plant his right foot as well, the shoe of the right foot fell off too, and both were found outside the church steps. Lucian marvelled at this. Epiphanius had no further intention of picking up the shoes that had fallen from his feet; nor, for the whole of his life, would he put any other shoes on his feet. As Epiphanius and his sister stood listening to the holy Scriptures, the bishop, seated on his throne, noticed that Epiphanius's face was glorified and that a crown had been placed on his head. So after the dismissal following the Gospel, the bishop went into the baptistery and ordered Epiphanius and his

sister to come in, and Lucian with them, who also became their godfather at holy baptism. The bishop taught them the whole order of the rite and baptized them. When they had received the divine and immortal mysteries, the bishop told them to dine with him and to stay the seven days in the bishop's residence as well. After the seven days, Epiphanius took Lucian and the holy virgin Bernice, who had become godmother to Epiphanius's sister, and brought them to his house. He took a thousand gold coins and gave them to Bernice, and entrusted his sister to her (for she was the superior of other virgins too), and sent his sister away with her. Epiphanius sold everything and distributed it to those in need, keeping forty gold coins for himself to acquire the divinely inspired and life-giving books; and he left the city with Lucian [?]. For Lucian had founded a monastery for himself, with ten monks under him, who earned their food by laboriously copying books. Epiphanius was sixteen years old when he became a monk. 9. In Lucian's monastery there was a monk named Hilarion, second to Lucian, who though young was adorned with many signs. Another monk, Claudius, followed his example. Seeing them, Epiphanius emulated them in what was good. Indeed the great Lucian entrusted Epiphanius to the most great Hilarion, so that he might teach him the divine Scriptures. Epiphanius applied himself diligently, and, moving about Hilarion's excellent ways as though in a paradise, he made progress by the grace of Christ and in the noblest of arts. Then the great Lucian departed this life, and Hilarion took charge of the company of the brothers. Truly one could see that place not as a dwelling of human beings but as a place of holy angels serving the God who loves humankind and is all-holy. The blessed Hilarion's food was bread, salt and a little water. He ate every second day, often every third, and very often every fourth day, or once a week. Epiphanius chose this way of life and held to it all the days of his life. The place was also waterless. 10. Once some travellers came to the monastery carrying wine. The heat was intense, and they stopped at the monastery to cool themselves in their great thirst. They asked for water to drink, but no water was to be found there, for the water was five miles away; the brothers would go at night and fill up for themselves. As the travellers were fainting from thirst, all the brothers grieved for them. But Epiphanius stretched out his hand, took hold of the skin that held the wine, and said, “Believe, brothers, that he who made the water wine will also make the wine water.” And at Epiphanius's word the skins that had been full of wine were found full of water. The travellers took it and drank, they and their animals too, and their life was restored

by it. All of them, travellers and brothers alike, were astounded at this. From that day Epiphanius no longer wished to live in that place, because the travellers had made him widely talked about. He stole away from the brothers and went to a wilder place. Not knowing where he was living, all the brothers mourned for Epiphanius. He stayed in that place three days without food; and that place too was waterless. 11. At that time it happened that forty Saracens were passing through. When they saw Epiphanius in such a place and in such a condition, they all made fun of him and mocked him. One of them, who had only one eye (the other was closed) and a beastly nature, drew his sword from its sheath and came at Epiphanius. But as he raised it to strike Epiphanius, his closed eye was opened. Seized with fear, he threw his sword on the ground and stood motionless. The others, seeing their comrade standing motionless, came up to Epiphanius and to their friend themselves. They looked, and there was his closed eye opened; and astonishment fell on all of them. When Epiphanius saw them distressed, he spoke with them at length. Calmed by Epiphanius's words, they changed their attitude and said that he was a god. They used force on him and dragged him along with them, saying, “You are our god; follow us and save us [?] from all the violence of those who rise up against us.” Epiphanius followed them for three months and restrained them from all disorder. Realizing that his admonitions were putting them under constraint, they all gathered together with one accord and rolled at his feet, begging him to go back to his own place. He laid the weightiest admonitions in their ears, saying, “Unless you abstain from these things, you cannot prosper in this life.” Then they all took him and brought him to the place where he had lived before; and having built him a dwelling with their own labour, they all embraced him and departed in peace. I, at any rate, being one of them, stayed with Epiphanius; and having been instructed by him in the word of truth, I remained with him. After six months had passed, Epiphanius took me and we went to the monastery, to the great Hilarion. When all the brothers saw Epiphanius, they rejoiced with great joy. We spent three days in the monastery, and Epiphanius asked the great Hilarion to give me the seal in Christ, since Hilarion had been deemed worthy of the rank of the priesthood. So the great Hilarion took me, taught me the whole order of the rite, and baptized me in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, directing that I be called John. We spent ten days with them, and the brothers begged Epiphanius to live together with them in that place. But he would not; he wanted to live again where he had lived before. (a) Perhaps read συνεῖρεν.

12. When we left the monastery, we went on our way. About two miles from the monastery we were met by a young man who had a demon of high rank and was being cut to pieces by it in the desert. When Epiphanius saw him naked and being driven about in a frenzied run by the unclean spirit, he cried out in a loud voice, “I command you in the name of the crucified Jesus Christ to come out of God's creature.” At once the unclean spirit convulsed the young man, threw him to the ground, and came out of him. The unclean demon cried out with a loud voice, “Epiphanius, you drive me out of my place after twenty-two years. I will go to the king of the Persians and stir him up against you, and I will make you stand before him in great affliction.” The young man came to his senses and fell at Epiphanius's feet. Epiphanius raised him up, saying, “Get up, child, and go home in peace.” And at once he got up. 13. The unclean demon went to Persia and attached itself to the king's daughter; and with the same torment with which it had seized the young man it tormented her too. And it cried out, saying, “Unless Epiphanius, who sent me away, comes here to your daughter, I will not come out of her.” And again the demon said, “Epiphanius, of the race of the Phoenicians, come here, so that I may come out of the king's daughter.” When the king heard the demon speak of Phoenicia, he sent a large number of fluent-speaking men to search for Epiphanius. They searched the whole country of the Phoenicians but did not find him, and returned to the king without success. Some of them were even badly treated by the Romans as spies who wanted to survey the whole land of Phoenicia with evil intent. The men who had been sent went and reported to the king that they had not found Epiphanius. But the demon cried out with a loud voice, “He is living in the place called Spanydrion.” So again the king summoned thirty men and said to them, “Take off Persian dress, put on Roman dress, and go to Phoenicia. Seek out the place called Spanydrion and bring me Epiphanius who lives there.” The thirty men sent by the king set out, having changed their clothes, and arrived in Phoenicia; and after much searching the place and Epiphanius were pointed out to them. They came to the place at night, while Epiphanius was offering his night prayers to God. When they stood at the door of the cell and knocked, Epiphanius was not at all disturbed in his thoughts, but went on completing the work of God. Filled with rage, they resolved to break down the door of the cell. One of them drew his sword and thrust it at the door's bolt-socket, and his hand remained motionless, immovable, and rigid, completely withered. All the others became terrified…

[?] they withdrew some distance from the cell. When Epiphanius had completed the whole order of the spiritual service, he opened the door of the cell. The man whose hand had withered saw him and fell on his face to the ground, saying, "Have mercy on me, initiate and servant of the immortals!" Epiphanius said, "What are you asking of a sinful man?" He said, "I came to this place healthy, and look, my hand has withered." Epiphanius said, "You came healthy; be healthy." And when he touched him, his hand was restored like the other. When all the others saw the sign that had taken place, they all came, fell down before Epiphanius and confessed why they had come to him. When he heard what the men said, he realized that the spirit he had driven out of the young man had gone and was afflicting the girl. Epiphanius said to me, "Get up, child; let us go with these men." They said to him, "Father, the king sent us to you alone, and we have brought a spare animal for you to ride." He said, "I run fast on foot; only I will not leave my disciple here." Again they said, in great fear, "There are camels for both of you; only be so kind as to follow your servants." Then a handsome young man fell on his face and bowed down to him, saying, "Forgive me, Father." Epiphanius, with a kindly face, said to him, "Get up; God will bless you, child." Then the young man, very composed, lifted Epiphanius in his two hands and set him on a racing camel. He came to me and did the same, and he himself rode at the head of the racing camels. 14 [?]. After we had travelled thirty-five stages, we reached the royal city and stayed at a place called Ourion. Three of them went in and announced us to the king. When the king ordered Epiphanius to come in to him, he went in quite composed, like one who had never had to meet a king. But I, walking behind him, was seized by fear and trembling; for when I saw the great crowds standing around him, my thoughts were shaken. As Epiphanius drew near the king, the king at once rose from his throne. Epiphanius said to the king, "Sit on your throne, child, and do not waver in your grief; for I have God as my helper, who drives out the devil. Only believe in the Lover of mankind; do not miss the meaning of what is said, and you will see your daughter healthy. For the most wicked demon, driven from one place, came eagerly upon your daughter. If you believe in the Crucified, he drives it out of your daughter. Let your heart be enlightened, child, and watch it being driven out. Bring her into our midst, and you will see the grace of the Lover of mankind." When the king's daughter came into the middle, Epiphanius said to the girl, "Come to your senses and bow down to your father. The wolf will no longer master you." Having said this, Epiphanius took the girl by the hand, sealed her three times with the sign of the cross, and said to the spirit afflicting her, "You did evil to run upon the king's daughter. Flee from her into uninhabited places." When Epiphanius had said this to the demon, it immediately came out of the girl.

Seeing the king in great amazement, Epiphanius said to him, "Rejoice over your daughter, king; the wolf has fled into uninhabited places. Go to your chamber, daughter, and be glad with your most excellent mother. From now on take care of your body, and no evildoer will come near you again." When the king's daughter heard this from Epiphanius, she went to the chamber where her mother was staying. Then the king bowed his neck before Epiphanius. When everyone saw the king, they too bowed to the ground, saying to Epiphanius, "You who are adorned with the grace of God, be well disposed toward the king, a father to his majesty, and stay with us always. A demon troubled the princess; you came here to drive it out." 15. Then one of them, one of the chief magi, said to him with goodwill, "O blessed Epiphanius, longed-for magus, you have come here to set things right. Teach everyone; all the magi will obey you." Hearing this, Epiphanius said to the foolish magus, "O magus, enemy of the truth, learn not to speak unruly words. Take a gag in your mouth, and stay without speaking for good. Do not suppose that a servant of God is a magus of unrighteousness." As soon as Epiphanius had said this, the magus stood there speechless and motionless on the spot. When the king and the retinue standing around him saw this, they were all seized with fear and fell to the ground. 16. Seeing them fallen, Epiphanius stretched out his hand to the king and said to him kindly, "Get up, compose yourself, and be well in your chamber." When Epiphanius had said this, they all rose to their feet. Epiphanius said to the magian, "Consider what you see and hear, [?] paying heed to the truth. Do not regard me as a magian, for I am a servant of the Crucified. Speak and hear as before, and become a friend of the truth." Then the magus apologized, telling Epiphanius that he had been mistaken. Then the king ordered gold, silver, pearls and precious stones to be brought before everyone and laid at Epiphanius's feet, saying to him, "Take these, our Father, and keep me in your heart." Epiphanius said to the king, "We despise all things so that we may hold fast to the truth; do not trouble me with the rest. Christ has taught me not to need such things. Take them yourself and bury them in your treasury, and they will be dead to you forever. You only pay attention to them and are distracted by them, without being able to profit from them. You have wickedness in your thoughts, destroying souls through the gold that the Lord gave you so that you might provide for those in need. Be righteous before the God of all, lest you be judged and condemned and kept under guard in the outer darkness, and only then remember my words. Accept my words now instead, and then you will rejoice. Have no need of this world, and the whole world will be subject to you. And beware of unstable magi, who deceive you with a law of darkness. The hour of the midday meal has come. Go

to the table with good cheer. I could have sown many words, but you would take in none of them; for I know your mind, that you never stray far from the table. Eat and enjoy yourself in moderation, for you will give an account of all these things." 17. The king said to Epiphanius, "Come, Father, let us sit down together and eat of the food." Epiphanius said to the king, "Go, sit at the table and eat everything as you usually do; only avoid excess. For me, bread made of bran and a little salt for good digestion will supply the body's need." When Epiphanius had said this to the king, the king dismissed everyone from the chamber, ordered us to go into the bedchamber, and sent us various dishes on a table. But Epiphanius sent everything back, keeping only one loaf for us. We ate it and were satisfied, giving thanks to the God of all. The next day the king sent for Epiphanius. He came in quite composed and went up very close to the king; and the king rose from his throne and laid the royal crown on the ground. Epiphanius said to the king, "Take up the dignity of your kingship, and be grateful to God." The king said to Epiphanius, "Stay here with us, Father, and I will keep your words." Epiphanius said to the king, "If you keep my words, I will remember you wherever I am." We spent ten days in the king's palace. Then Epiphanius said to the king, "I am setting out for my homeland, for I am seeking all who are there [?]. And you, stay seated on your throne and do not rise up against the Romans. For if you are hostile to the Romans, you will be hostile to the Crucified; and if you become an enemy of the one who was crucified, you will waste away miserably at the hands of your adversaries." When Epiphanius had said this to the king, the king rode out first with his retinue, escorting us into the countryside. 18. As we came out of the palace, there was a young man lying dead on a bier, the son of one of the nobles. They were carrying him off to the [?] dogs, to throw him out to be devoured. Epiphanius said kindly to the bearers of the bier, "Set him down on the ground, children. Let us too look at the dead man. This boy died wretchedly through sorcery, at the hands of an evildoer." It is the custom among the Persians for the dead to be eaten. When they at once set the bier on the ground, Epiphanius said to the king, "O king of kings, [king] of wicked [?] and lawless men! This man, having departed this life, ought to have been buried safely in the earth, so that the Master, sounding the trumpet from heaven, might raise him up again to worship. Yet you rule over men so unruly that they even bring death on themselves before its time. Look: this man whom you see dead departed this life through an evildoer. But my God, who was stretched out on the wood, will raise him up before everyone." When Epiphanius had said this, and

had felt the dead man with his hands, he cried out to the Lover of mankind, "Son of God, who raised Lazarus from the dead after four days, raise up this young man!" And Epiphanius took his own outer garment and clothed the dead man in it; for it was the custom among the Persians to carry the dead naked. At once the young man rose and embraced Epiphanius. Epiphanius said to the young man, "Go to your house, child, and put on your usual clothes; and bring me back my outer garment." For it was Epiphanius's custom to wear a tunic of hair next to his flesh and the outer garment over it. When the king saw what had happened through Epiphanius, he supposed him to be a god. Epiphanius said to the king, "Do not attribute these things to me; I am a man of like passions with you. It is my God, in whom I have believed, who grants these things to his friends." When Epiphanius had said this and more besides, he said to the king, "Go back to your palace, child; we are going to our homeland." The king said to Epiphanius, "How many swordsmen shall I send to keep you safe, Father?" Epiphanius said to the king, "I have God in heaven guarding me, and his holy angels as swordsmen." Then the king embraced Epiphanius and cried out with a loud voice, "Go in good health, Epiphanius, glory of the Romans, and remember us in Persia." Setting out from Persia, we went into Phoenicia; and having passed through part of Phoenicia, we came to Spanydrion. We found the cell as it had been before. By the third day there was no water for us to drink. 19. So Epiphanius stood facing east and prayed to God in heaven, saying, "You who split the sheer rock and made water gush out of it, and gave drink to a people who lacked water, tear open this ground too, and make water spring from it for poor men to live here." When Epiphanius had said this, a sweet fragrance filled that place. Again he bowed three times to the ground and prayed; then he took a digging tool and scratched the ground a little, and a trickle of water welled up. Then he dug again, and our dwelling became rich in streams. We lived in that place in stillness, he and I. And God, who makes grass grow for the cattle and green plants for the service of men—as the water irrigated all that land, by the command of him who always provides for the human race—made the earth bring forth an abundance of vegetables for our enjoyment and sustenance. But when some wild animals came at them and were destroying all the greenery, Epiphanius stood over the vegetables and spoke to the animals as if to men, saying, "Do not trouble me; I am a sinful and poor man. It is because of the multitude of my sins that I am in this

place, mourning. God has granted me this comfort of vegetables for my sustenance, and he himself commands you not to come to this place any more and damage my greenery." When the wild beasts heard this from Epiphanius, they behaved like sensitive people who, if they offend some great person and are rebuked, are put to shame: so the beasts were abashed by Epiphanius's words and withdrew at once, and from that day they never again came near our place. When the Saracens who had built the cell for us heard that Epiphanius had come back from Persia, they came to meet him so as to be blessed by him. They built three more houses for us, spending [?] months with us, and then went back to their own places. It became known throughout the whole city (Phoenicia) that Epiphanius was living at Spanydrion, and so other brothers gathered in the monastery. Altogether we numbered eight. 20. One day Epiphanius went to the monastery of the great Hilarion to visit the brothers, and I went with him. The brothers received us with great joy and kept us for many days. Then the devil, who from the beginning has opposed the servants of God, took on the appearance of Epiphanius and went to the monastery called Spanydrion. One of the more careless brothers met him and ran to bow down before him; and falling to the ground, he bowed down to the most wicked demon. It entered into him, and he became uncontrollable among the brothers. Epiphanius said to the great Hilarion, "A wolf has got into the monastery, Father; it has troubled and shaken all the brothers." Having said this, Epiphanius embraced everyone, and we set out on our way. Another time three peasants came into the monastery, and one of them had an unclean demon. The other two pleaded with Epiphanius for the one who had the unclean spirit, saying, "Help our companion." Epiphanius said to them, "Take your friend, children, and go in peace; for in the name of Jesus Christ there is nothing evil in him." They believed Epiphanius's word, and the man went away to his house healthy. 21. Once there was a lion in a desert place about sixty miles from our monastery. It lay hidden in a wood and killed many of the people passing through that place. Now this place was a convenient route for travellers. So all who were accustomed to pass through that place gathered and came to Epiphanius at the monastery, telling him about the beast and its wicked savagery, and that the place had become deserted and impassable. "Father," they said, "this is from fear of the lion, because it has killed many people;

and the rest are terrified and no longer want to pass through that place." When Epiphanius heard about the lion's savagery, he said to all who were present, "Let us go, children, in the name of the Lord, and we shall see this bloodthirsty lion." Epiphanius took me, and we went with the men. When we arrived, great fear fell on all who were with us. Epiphanius said to the men, "Where, children, is the lion's lair?" When they pointed out the place, Epiphanius went ahead of everyone. Since the lion was nowhere to be seen, Epiphanius said in a loud voice, "Where is the lair of the lawless lion?" The lion leaped out of the wood to meet Epiphanius. But the moment it saw Epiphanius, it fell to the ground and lay dead. When Epiphanius went up close to its mouth, they all fled, seized with great fear, thinking it might kill Epiphanius too. But Epiphanius called out to them all in a loud voice, "Come, children, without fear, and you will see the carcass of the beast." They all gathered at once, and everyone saw the beast's carcass. Epiphanius said to the men, "If you have faith in the Savior, all who plot against you will fall like this." Then all the men took us and brought us safely back to the monastery, and after being blessed by Epiphanius they went their own way. 22. The place formerly called Spanydrion was made glorious through Epiphanius. It had once been uninhabited, impassable and waterless; that is why it had been given the name Spanydrion, from its having no water. But it became a paradise sharing in every good thing, with an abundance of water and of all kinds of food. Then, besides all these things of which Epiphanius was counted worthy by God, God granted him this great and wonderful gift: to interpret the divine Scriptures with complete truth. For he would take the divine books and read them to the brothers, and show them their full meaning. Now Epiphanius the great rhetor, who was also a philosopher and lived in Edessa, heard that Epiphanius was a learned man, and he longed to come and meet him. When he arrived at the monastery, the crowd of brothers was standing and sending up hymns to God, while Epiphanius was saying his prayers on his own. After the whole service was over, Epiphanius appeared before the brothers. The rhetor was standing and watching the crowd, having greeted no one. When the philosopher saw Epiphanius, he recognized him, ran up and bowed down to him. Epiphanius said to the philosopher, "Why, great Epiphanius, great rhetor—why have you come to the least and most sinful of men, little Epiphanius? This is what amazes me, philosopher: why have you come to an unlearned man, and by so long a road at that? For what reason? Tell me, philosopher." The philosopher said to Epiphanius, "Do not be amazed at this, longed-for teacher. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus used to say that faces

looking upon one another can grow most beautiful, or else the bad, mixed with the good, will be stretched out on one wood [?]. For no man who wears only one tunic will keep his body unscratched. Much company yields many words, and where there are many words, there is wide experience of all sorts of matters." When the philosopher had said this and more to Epiphanius, he fell silent and said nothing further. 23. Epiphanius then took up the first book, on the making of the world, and interpreted it to the philosopher word by word. The philosopher accepted some things and disputed others. They spent three days in discussion with each other, and they did not agree on what they said. But when the philosopher saw Epiphanius's way of life and character, he came to love him greatly. On the fourth day the philosopher said to Epiphanius, "Teacher, this place is a fine place to live. If you allow it, I would like to live here." Epiphanius said to the philosopher, "That is a matter for each person's own choice." The philosopher said to Epiphanius, "But I will bring my books too." He said to him, "Whatever comes into your mind, you will find Epiphanius agreeable." The philosopher said, "Callistus will go for my books." Epiphanius said to the philosopher, "Bring them; go in good health with Callistus." The philosopher said to Epiphanius, "I leave all my affairs to Callistus; for I will never again leave this place." Now Callistus was the son of Aetius, the great prefect of Rome. He had an evil spirit, and he saw Epiphanius in a vision saying to him, "Callistus, do you want me to drive the spirit out of you?" Callistus said, "And who are you, my lord, that you can drive it out?" Epiphanius said to Callistus, "I am Epiphanius the Phoenician-Palestinian, who lives in the monastery at Spanydrion. If I drive the evil spirit out of you, you will come and live with me at Spanydrion." Callistus said to Epiphanius, "Lord, drive the unclean spirit out of me, and I will live with you." Epiphanius said to Callistus, "See that you do not do otherwise, or it will cling to you again." When Callistus woke up, he told his father, the prefect. From that day on Callistus was no longer afflicted by the unclean spirit. After three months he said to his father Aetius, "Father, I want to go to the land of the Phoenicians, seek out Epiphanius and live with him at Spanydrion." His father at once gave him a great deal of money and sent him off with an escort. He came to Phoenicia, sought out Epiphanius, explained everything to him, and lived with us. So the philosopher, at Epiphanius's bidding, sent Callistus to Edessa with two servants and three camels to bring his books to the monastery. Callistus made the journey to Edessa, took the philosopher's books, loaded them onto the three camels, and came back to the monastery.

24 [?]. Every day, then, Epiphanius and the philosopher were locked in fierce argument with each other. Epiphanius said to the philosopher, “Philosopher, Daniel says that the court sat and the books were opened. Come,” he said, “set out your books, and I will set out mine, which God has graciously given me, and let us sit down and have our case judged between us.” Epiphanius placed the divinely inspired Scriptures on the right, and the philosopher placed his books on the left. They began from the beginning, with the making of the world: Epiphanius from the Genesis that Moses wrote, and the philosopher from the account of the same origins that Hesiod wrote. They went through the two books line by line, arguing with each other. And the light was light, and the darkness darkness. For Moses wrote with God working alongside him, while Hesiod had his life from God but his error from demons. Epiphanius spent a whole year debating with the philosopher and did not persuade him. Then one day some peasants, sixty of them, brought a young man who was troubled by the unclean spirit. Since the sixty could not overpower him, they had bound him with chains, and they brought him to Epiphanius at the monastery. Epiphanius said to the philosopher, “Come now, philosopher, you who keep up your arguments with the sinner Epiphanius: call upon the multitude of your gods, so that they may drive the spirit out of the young man.” The philosopher supposed that Epiphanius had been beaten and had run out of arguments. Epiphanius saw this and said to the philosopher, “What do you say about the young man, philosopher? Either you heal the sick man, and I will put my faith in your gods, or my God will drive the unclean spirit out of the young man, and you will put your trust in the Crucified.” Despite all this the philosopher did not believe Epiphanius, but thought the whole thing ridiculous. So Epiphanius stood up, took hold of the young man and said to him, “I say to you, young man: do you want me to [?] the irons from your hands?” 25. When the philosopher heard this, he immediately ran into his cell and secured the door with the bolt. He said to himself, full of suspicion, “This monk, being an unlearned man, means to set the madman loose. Unless we, as learned men, escape his recklessness, we are going to suffer badly at the hands of that accursed creature.” Epiphanius lifted the irons off the young man, sealed him three times with the sign of the cross, and said to the unclean spirit, “Epiphanius the sinner, the servant of the Lord, commands you in the name of Jesus Christ the Crucified, the Son of God: come out of the man, and never enter him again.” At once the unclean spirit came out, and the young man was completely calm. When the philosopher saw that all was peaceful, he drew back the bolt and leapt out of the cell to prostrate himself before Epiphanius, saying to him, “O Epiphanius, crowned victor, I believe, and have come to believe, what you have said, because of the

deeds that have been done. For words fly away without bearing fruit, but deeds show that they bear fruit. I too want to belong to the Crucified.” Epiphanius said to the philosopher, “Why are you amazed at this, philosopher, as though we had done it? No: it is the Son of God who does these good things through those who believe in him.” When Epiphanius had said these things and many more to the philosopher, the philosopher begged him to give him the seal in Christ. Epiphanius took him, and me as well, and we went to the great Hilarion, and he baptized him. We spent twenty days in the monastery of the great Hilarion. Epiphanius asked the great Hilarion to send one of the brothers to Eleutheropolis with Epiphanius, the former philosopher, so that the bishop might ordain him a presbyter. And the great Hilarion did so. Then we went back to our monastery, which is called Spanydrion. Epiphanius called all the brothers together and said to them, “This man once thought he was something when he was nothing, and called himself a philosopher. But now by the grace of Christ he has become a true philosopher and has been found worthy of the priesthood. This is your spiritual father.” So Epiphanius, the former philosopher, was granted a gift of grace from God, and he became the head of the whole community. 26. Many people kept coming to the monastery and would not leave Epiphanius in peace. So he decided to leave the place and go to the region of Egypt, and he said to me, “Child, follow me.” I said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go, Father.” He called all the brothers together and took his leave of them, giving them this explanation: “Children, I am going to visit the brothers in the monastery of the great Hilarion.” But they understood that he meant to withdraw because of the great disturbance caused by the visitors, and they all fell on their faces and, weeping and lamenting bitterly, begged Epiphanius not to leave. Epiphanius was himself moved to great pity, and he reassured them by saying that he would not withdraw after all. But before ten days had passed, he took me by night, and we left and went to Jerusalem and venerated our life, the precious cross of the [?]. We spent sixteen days in the city, going round the holy places and praying. As we were leaving the city to sail for Egypt, we met a woman who was raving under an unclean spirit. She grabbed Epiphanius's cloak and tore it, and at once the unclean spirit came out of her. She fell at Epiphanius's feet and pleaded with him, “Forgive me, Father, and do not be angry.” Epiphanius said to the woman, “Go home in good health, for the one who did the tearing has been torn.” And the woman went home. When we went down to Joppa, we found a ship ready to sail for Alexandria. When we had disembarked and entered the city, a Jew named Aquila, a teacher of the Law, met us. And Epiphanius

began to debate with them from the Law as well. They argued fiercely all that day. The next day they met again and held a discussion with each other, until Aquila was persuaded by Epiphanius's interpretation and longed to become a Christian. Epiphanius looked after him and brought him to Pope Athanasius, and we left the city of Alexandria. As we were travelling toward the region of the Upper Thebaid, we met a monk named Paphnutius, a disciple of the great Antony. Epiphanius said to him, “Bless us, Father.” Paphnutius said, “You are blessed by the Lord.” When Paphnutius had said the prayer, we greeted one another and rested a little in that place. Epiphanius asked Paphnutius about everything the great Antony had done, and he told him all of it. Epiphanius said to Paphnutius, “Father, I want to live in the place called Nitria.” Paphnutius said to Epiphanius, “Go in good health. Enjoy the company of the fathers, gather summer hay, and then go to the island of Cyprus. Raise sheep for clothing, and cherish the young, so that there may be lambs.” When Paphnutius had said this, we prayed again, greeted one another, and each went his own way. 27. In the region around Leontopolis there was a man whom some considered good and gifted by God with foreknowledge. His name was Hieracas. Epiphanius had heard about him in Palestine and longed to see him, and Hieracas had likewise heard about Epiphanius. He lived about a mile outside Leontopolis. He taught that this flesh does not rise, but another flesh in its place, and that this one dissolves into earth, because it is written, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return.” He also said that children would not be made perfect in the age to come. When we entered his monastery, we found great crowds being taught by him, for he practiced severe abstinence from food and drink: from the time he renounced the world he had taken neither oil nor wine. When he saw Epiphanius, he asked where he was from. When he learned that he was a Palestinian, he asked his name as well, and when he learned that he was called Epiphanius, he became very anxious. For people in Egypt said of Epiphanius that he was learned and had foreknowledge. After he had asked Epiphanius where he was from and what he was called, and had found out, he went back to teaching the crowd. When he came to expound the resurrection, he said of the flesh that it does not rise. Epiphanius was distressed and said to Hieracas, “Put a bolt on your mouth, and learn not to blaspheme against our hope.” At Epiphanius's word Hieracas stayed where he was, speechless and motionless. When all those he was teaching saw the miracle Epiphanius had worked on Hieracas, they were astonished. Then Epiphanius took up the subject and began to teach them all about the resurrection from the divine Scriptures. About

three hours passed, and Hieracas remained without a voice. After this Epiphanius said to him, “Speak the word of truth, and listen to the firm faith.” Then Hieracas made his defence, telling Epiphanius that he had been mistaken, but that he repented of that disordered opinion. 28. Setting out from Leontopolis, we went to the Upper Thebaid. There was a righteous man there named John. We went to him, and he received us kindly. Some people from those parts had tied up a young man near him to wait [?]. He was troubled by an unclean spirit. When he saw Epiphanius, he said to him in a loud voice, “Why have you come here, Epiphanius, servant of God?” He kept crying out like this from the sixth hour to the ninth. Then suddenly he burst his bonds and ran to Epiphanius. He seized his feet and cried out, “Release me, for the sake of the God whom you worship!” Now Epiphanius had told the unclean spirit not to come out of the man, so that John would not find out about him. Epiphanius said to the young man, “Get up, man. Why are you giving me trouble?” At once the young man stood up, healthy, for the unclean spirit had gone out of him. We stayed three days with John, a wonderful man adorned with a virtuous way of life. Setting out from there, we went down to the Boukolia and spent seven years there. There too people gave Epiphanius much trouble with their visits. 29. One day a philosopher named Eudaemon came to Epiphanius, and they took up arguments against each other. They spent ten days debating. Epiphanius demonstrated the truth to Eudaemon from the divinely inspired Scriptures, while Eudaemon, out of useless love of argument, contradicted everything Epiphanius said. Eudaemon had a child, one of whose eyes was closed. Epiphanius said to Eudaemon, “Look, philosopher, you are richly endowed in every way, with eloquence and with wealth, and you have gods in abundance. Why do you not take care of your child, so that both his eyes may be healthy?” At this the philosopher laughed and said to Epiphanius, “If Eudaemon's child were the only one under heaven with a single eye, I might have worried about him. But since countless people go about on this earth without even one eye, why should Eudaemon care about this?” Epiphanius said to Eudaemon, “But if he were the only one, philosopher, what could you have done to cure him?” Eudaemon said, “Nothing, except to tell myself often, and say aloud, that there has never been anyone like our child.” Epiphanius said to him, “Do not treat what I say as a joke, philosopher, for God stands between the two of us. Bring the maimed child, and see the glory of God.” When he had said this, Epiphanius took

Eudaemon's child by the hand and sealed his unseeing eye three times with the sign of the cross, and at once the boy received his sight. When Eudaemon saw what Epiphanius had done, he pleaded with him, “If it please you, teacher, I too want to become a Christian.” He said to him, “Listen, philosopher, to what I tell you about the good and compassionate God in whom Christians believe. Once, when Israel was enslaved to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, he set them free and delivered them from him. He led them through the sea and through the desert, and brought them into a land flowing with milk and honey. And when they disobeyed and forgot God, he appealed to them through the prophet, saying, ‘My people, what have I done to you? How have I wronged you, or how have I burdened you? Answer me.’ So, learned Eudaemon, God is ready to welcome all who come to him in good faith, and even if someone has committed a great many sins, he will be forgiven. [?] then, learned Eudaemon, go into the city, and do not be ashamed to fall down before the bishop. For Christ loves humility, and that is why he came to us in great humility.” 30. Eudaemon heeded Epiphanius's words. He went into the city, fell down before the bishop, and became a Christian. Epiphanius became famous throughout all Egypt. The bishops tried to seize him and make him a bishop, but the One who guides was guiding Epiphanius. For Epiphanius knew of this and said to me, “Come, child, let us go back to our homeland.” So we went back to our homeland and entered the monastery of the great Hilarion. But the great Hilarion had withdrawn from the monastery because of the great disturbance he was suffering, and had sailed away to the region around Paphos in Cyprus. When the brothers saw Epiphanius, they were overjoyed, for they had been mourning for the great Hilarion. We spent forty days in that monastery, and then left and went to our own monastery, called Spanydrion, where Epiphanius had made Epiphanius of Edessa abbot. This man had gathered a great number of brothers in the monastery, for he was himself a wonderful man. When they [?] Epiphanius, they were all overjoyed. He and I spent three days in the monastery, lodging together in one place. On the fourth day he said to me, “Child, take another cell and live there in stillness.” I did so, and we lived in stillness in the monastery. 31. When a famine struck that region, in the land of Phoenicia, great crowds gathered to Epiphanius and pleaded with him, “Help us, Father, so that we do not perish. Pray to God to send rain on the land, so that the land may yield its harvest.” Epiphanius said to the people, “Why do you trouble me? I am a sinful man.” But they begged Epiphanius all the more to pray to God, the lover of

humankind. Epiphanius said to them, “I have already told you that I am a sinner.” As they kept on pleading, the ninth hour of the day arrived. Epiphanius said to the abbot, “Tell the brothers to set a table for these people, so that they may eat and be refreshed and go on their way.” They set a table, and Epiphanius went into his cell. While they were eating, the sun was sending down its rays as in summer. Suddenly darkness fell, and there was lightning and thunder, and heavy rain came down on the land. They all got up from the table in fear. There was no place in all Phoenicia that did not receive the blessing. The rain kept on for three days without stopping. Then the men came to Epiphanius's dwelling and pleaded with him, “Stop the rain from heaven with a word from your mouth.” Epiphanius said to them, “Why do you attribute these things to me, children? I am a man just like you. Our Benefactor knows what we need. Do you want to go on your way?” They said, “Yes, Father.” When he came out of his cell, they all gathered and surrounded him. Epiphanius again said to the abbot, “Give the word, and let them set a table for the people, so that they may eat and drink and go their way.” When they had all sat down at table, they asked Epiphanius to say the blessing. As soon as Epiphanius said, “Blessed is the Lord,” the rain stopped falling on the land. Once again Epiphanius saw how much disturbance he was suffering in the monastery, and once again he sought to withdraw. 32. One day the bishops held a meeting about choosing a bishop, and they thought of Epiphanius. Among the bishops there was a monk named Polybius, a devout man, young in years but perfect in self-control. He knew Epiphanius. The bishops said to him, “Take a swift mount, go to the monastery, and see whether Epiphanius is there; then hurry back and tell us. But tell no one about this, not even Epiphanius himself.” So Polybius came to the monastery, went in, and greeted Epiphanius. Epiphanius said to Polybius, “Why have you come here, my child Polybius?” Polybius said to Epiphanius, “Father, I want to run alongside the truth.” Epiphanius said to Polybius, “You have run, you have come, my child Polybius, sent by holy men to spy. Do not hide it, child; lying is evil. Tell the truth, for God stands between us. Be a tested servant of the truth. Epiphanius goes about from place to place, groaning and trembling because of his sins. But come now, Polybius, stay here, send the mount back to the priests, and leave the priests to look for men worthy of the sees.” When Epiphanius had said this to Polybius, Polybius at once accepted his word. He took leave of his attendant and sent the mount back to the bishops. And the One who guides was guiding Epiphanius toward Cyprus. That night he took me and Polybius

with him, and we left the monastery and went to Jerusalem to venerate our life, the precious cross. We entered the city and spent three days there. Epiphanius said to me and Polybius, “Come, let us go and receive a blessing from our father, the great Hilarion, for I have heard that he is in Cyprus.” And the One who guides was guiding Epiphanius. 33. When we went down to Caesarea, we found a Cypriot ship there from the city of Paphos. Epiphanius asked the ship's master where the great Hilarion was living. He told him that Hilarion lived in a cave in the countryside around Paphos, and that there in Paphos he was asking for our ship [?]. That night we went on board and sailed to Paphos. We disembarked, asked our way, and reached the great Hilarion. When we came in, there was great joy at the meeting, and we stayed in that place two months. Hilarion was much troubled by the people who came to him. When Epiphanius decided that we should leave Paphos, Hilarion said to him, “Where are you going, child?” Epiphanius said to Hilarion, “To Ascalon, to Gaza, and on into the land beyond.” Hilarion said to Epiphanius, “Go to Salamis, child, and you will find a place to live there.” But Epiphanius did not want to heed Hilarion's words. So Hilarion said to Epiphanius again, “I have told you, child, that you must go there and live there. So do not argue against our words, or you may also meet with danger at sea.” So we said our farewells and went down to the sea, where we found two ships: one crossing to Ascalon, the other sailing to Salamis. We boarded the ship that was to sail for Ascalon, but a great storm arose at sea, and the ship was in danger of breaking apart. We spent three days at sea, having given up hope for ourselves. On the fourth day the crew ran the ship before the oncoming waves, and they brought us to the city of Salamis. When everyone had disembarked, they all lay on the ground like dead men from their great distress and lack of food. The ship stayed at the place to be repaired, [?] from the violence of the waves. After we had spent three days there, by the grace of God we recovered, and once again Epiphanius wanted us to sail away from the place. Now the bishop of the place, I mean of the city of Salamis, had departed this life. 34. All the bishops of the island had gathered to ordain someone able to shepherd the flock of Christ. They had spent days together, praying to Christ to reveal to them the man able to serve in the priesthood. Among the bishops was a holy man who had been ordained bishop of a poor town called Kythrea, twenty-five miles from the city of Salamis. It was said that he had held the episcopate for fifty-eight years. He had also been counted worthy to bear witness for the faith: he suffered much for Christ and was released after confessing the Son of God. It was said that he had been arrested along with Gelasius, bishop of the city of Salamis, for martyr-

[?]…tyresai. The name given to him at birth (a) by his parents was Pappus, and he too was one of the bishops. All the bishops regarded him as a father, both for his confession of Christ and for his many years as a bishop. He also had foreknowledge from God. It was revealed to him that Epiphanius was to be ordained bishop of the church of Salamis. It was summer, the season just before the grapes ripen. When Epiphanius decided that we should sail from the city of Salamis, he said to me and to Polybius, “Come, child, let us go to the market and buy grapes for the voyage.” When we had come to the market and were bargaining with the seller, Epiphanius picked up two very fine bunches and said to the seller, “What do you want me to give you for the two bunches?” It was Epiphanius’s habit never to haggle. When the seller had told Epiphanius the price of the grapes, he took out the money to give it to the seller. Just then the holy Pappus arrived, [?] by two deacons, and three bishops were with him. As they came up to Epiphanius, he was holding the bunches and the money for them. Some of the bystanders said, “Look, the bishops are here.” Pappus said to Epiphanius, “Give the bunches back to the seller, Abba, and follow us into the church.” Remembering the divine word that calls out, “I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let us go to the house of the Lord,’” he followed them into the church. Then Pappus said to Epiphanius, “Say a prayer, Father.” Pappus said this so that Epiphanius would make himself known to the clergy. Epiphanius said to Pappus, “Forgive me, Father, but I am not one of the clergy.” Pappus said to Epiphanius, “Take care, my child, that you do not refuse in the presence of these holy fathers and be condemned like the man who hid his talent.” Epiphanius said to Pappus, “No, Father, for I am not a cleric.” When Epiphanius had said this, Pappus gave the peace. Then one of the deacons seized Epiphanius by the head and dragged him by force to Pappus at the altar, so that a great many others gathered to hold him fast at the altar. So Pappus ordained him deacon, and again gave the peace, and… (a) Perhaps “from birth.”

…at the disclosure of the bishop. And all of them kept troubling me, sinner that I am, saying, ‘Pray earnestly, and it will be revealed to you.’ 35. So I shut myself up in a room and pleaded with the Saviour about this matter. A flash of lightning lit up the cell, and I heard a voice speaking to me, the sinner: ‘Pappus, Pappus, listen.’ Terrified, I said, ‘What does my Lord command?’ And he said to me kindly, ‘Get up, take one of the deacons with you, and go down to the market. There you will find a monk at the seller’s stall buying grapes. He has two monks with him, and his head looks like Elisha’s. Ordain him bishop. But do not tell him beforehand, or he may run away. His name is Epiphanius.’ I have become a fool, my child; you forced me to it. Be careful what you do, and watch yourself. I was sent; I have done what I had to do. I am innocent. You must see to all the rest.” When Epiphanius heard this, he fell on his face and bowed down before Pappus, saying, “Do not be angry, Father, for I am a sinful man and not equal to the dignity of the priesthood.” After bowing to them all, he urged them to stay for the meal. When they had eaten, each of them went back to his own church. 36. Three days later a respectable man named Eugnomon was thrown into prison by one of the most prominent men of the city over a debt of a hundred gold coins. The man who had him imprisoned was called Draco. This Eugnomon was a Roman and had no one to get him out of prison. Epiphanius heard of it and went to Draco to ask him to release Eugnomon the Roman from prison. Draco said to Epiphanius, “Go away, you interloper in our city! Your friend owes me a hundred gold coins; give them to me and take him.” This Draco was very rich and savage in his ways. So Epiphanius went to the bishop’s residence. A hundred gold coins were kept there for the service of the Church. Epiphanius took them, went and gave them to Draco, and set the stranger free. Now there was a deacon named Charinus, whom many people testified to be unruly. He stirred up all the clergy against Epiphanius, saying, “Come, let us drive out this stranger before he eats up everything the Church owns and we become guilty of the sin.” This Charinus was very rich, and he was trying to drive out Epiphanius so that he himself could sit on the bishop’s throne. So they confronted Epiphanius, and Charinus spoke these words: “Was it not enough for you, Epiphanius, that you came here without so much as a cloak and took over the Church? Must you also squander the Church’s property, stranger that you are? Who is going to put up with this? Either give back the Church’s hundred gold coins or go back to your own country.” Meanwhile the Roman whom Epiphanius had freed went to Rome, sold everything he owned, and brought the money to Epiphanius. Epiphanius took it and gave it away to those in need. The Roman stayed

[?]…tyresai. The name given to him at birth (a) by his parents was Pappus, and he too was one of the bishops. All the bishops regarded him as a father, both for his confession of Christ and for his many years as a bishop. He also had foreknowledge from God. It was revealed to him that Epiphanius was to be ordained bishop of the church of Salamis. It was summer, the season just before the grapes ripen. When Epiphanius decided that we should sail from the city of Salamis, he said to me and to Polybius, “Come, child, let us go to the market and buy grapes for the voyage.” When we had come to the market and were bargaining with the seller, Epiphanius picked up two very fine bunches and said to the seller, “What do you want me to give you for the two bunches?” It was Epiphanius’s habit never to haggle. When the… (a) Perhaps “from birth.”

with Epiphanius until the day of his death. Epiphanius took the hundred gold coins and gave them to Charinus, saying to him, “Take the hundred gold coins I spent on the stranger.” Charinus, shameless as a dog, took the coins from Epiphanius, and calling together all the clergy he said to them, “Come and take the hundred gold coins that Epiphanius squandered; I have made him pay back every one.” But the clergy did not go along with Charinus’s malice. They said to him, “Go and give them back to the one you took them from.” Even so, he did not give them back to Epiphanius. Charinus treated Epiphanius very badly in a great many ways, yet Epiphanius never once held it against him.

37. Once, at a meal in the bishop’s residence, Epiphanius had all the clergy at his table. It was Epiphanius’s habit to hold the holy Gospels in his hands and teach the divine word night and day. While Epiphanius was teaching those at table, a bird called a raven let out a loud cry. Charinus said to the diners, “Which of you knows what the raven said?” But Epiphanius went on speaking the divine word. The raven gave the same cry again, and again Charinus said, “Which of you knows what the raven is saying?” And again Epiphanius went on teaching everyone at the meal. Then the raven cried out a third time. Again Charinus said to those at the meal, “I asked you: which of you knows what the raven is saying?” Then Epiphanius, not in the least disturbed but with great composure, said to Charinus, “I know what the raven said.” Charinus said, “Tell me, and you shall be master of everything I own.” Epiphanius said to Charinus, “The raven said that you are not to be a deacon.” At Epiphanius’s word Charinus was seized with trembling. He spoke no more, and neither ate nor drank anything. His servants carried him home and laid him on a bed, and at dawn he died in his bed. He had a most faithful wife, but she had no child (a). She brought everything she had to Epiphanius, and he made her a deaconess of the Church. Her hand had been paralysed for ten years. When Epiphanius took hold of her to seal her with the sign of the cross, she was healed at once and freed from her pain. From the day that Epiphanius spoke to Charinus, and at his word Charinus received his sentence from the Lord, all the clergy submitted to Epiphanius with fear and trembling. 38. For this too was granted to the blessed man: at the time of the offering he never completed the offering until he had seen the vision. The blessed man would say the words, and at once it would be revealed to him. Once, however, after he had said the words a third time, the vision did not come. He grieved and prayed that the cause might be made known to him, and he looked first at the deacon on his left,

who was holding the liturgical fan. As he looked at him, Epiphanius saw leprosy spreading over his forehead. It was plain to everyone that he was not without guilt. So Epiphanius reached out his hand and took the liturgical fan from him, saying to him kindly, “Go home, my child, and do not receive the divine mysteries just now.” He went out at once and went home. Epiphanius gave the fan to another deacon. Then he began the divine words again with fear and tears, and when he had finished, he saw the vision at once. After the dismissal of the congregation, Epiphanius called the deacon and questioned him, wanting to learn the cause. When the deacon said that he had slept with his wife that night, Epiphanius called together all the

“…children,” he said, “you have been counted worthy of the clergy. Set aside your marriage crowns, so as not to go back to them, and so serve the holy man who preaches in the churches, saying, ‘Let those who have wives be as though they had none.’” From then on Epiphanius no longer ordained anyone who had a wife, but only holy men who followed the solitary life, and men of proven character. Truly, one could see the Church like a beautiful bride, adorned by her priesthood.

BY POLYBIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF RHINOCORURA: ON THE REST OF THE LIFE OF OUR HOLY FATHER EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF CONSTANTIA. 39. Glory to the God of all, who gives us life and glorifies those who glorify him, as the divine word says: “Those who glorify me I will glorify, and whoever despises me will be dishonoured.” It happened that John, the holy father, fell ill with the illness from which he died. When he was confined to his bed, he called me and said to me, “Polybius, my child.” I said to him, “What do you wish, Father?” He said to me, “Since Epiphanius forbids anyone to write down what God has accomplished through him, take these papers. Up to today I have been writing down what I saw Epi- [Patrol. Gr. XLI]

-phanius do, without his knowing. Now you too, my child, must record what follows from this day on. For God means to grant you the span of Epiphanius’s life (a); you will stay with him through it. But see that you do not neglect this, for I too wrote these things because God moved me to. Now I am going the way of all the earth.” When he had said this, John said to me, “Call our holy father Epiphanius to me.” I went and called him. When he came in, Epiphanius said to John, “Father John, you are neglecting to pray for the sinner Epiphanius.” John said to Epiphanius, “Say a prayer, Father, for I have something to tell you.” So Epiphanius said the prayer. When everyone had said the Amen, John said to Epiphanius, “Come close to me, Father.” And he came close to him. John said to Epiphanius, “Lay your hands on my eyes and kiss me, Father, for I am departing.” Epiphanius laid his hands on his eyes and kissed him. And John gave up his spirit. Epiphanius fell on John’s neck and wept for him, and he grieved over John’s death. 40. Once Epiphanius fell on his face to entreat God to help him build a house for his name, for the first church was too small for those who came. As he lay on his face praying to God about the need for a church, the voice of God came to him: “Epiphanius.” Epiphanius was used to hearing such a voice often, so he was not alarmed and said, “What is it, my God?” And the voice said, “Begin building the house.” At once, without delay, Epiphanius went out, said the prayer and the whole service for the site, and set the builders to work. There were sixty master builders for the building of the house, and great crowds of workers to assist them. At that time there were pagans in the city, rich men who owned money and property. 41. One of them was called Draco, and most people called him Draco the Great. He had a son, also called Draco. The son suffered in his right side from a terrible fever. His father had spent a great deal on doctors but had gained nothing toward his son’s health. Now Draco the Great showed much hostility to Epiphanius in word and deed, but whenever Epiphanius saw him, he was the first to bow to him. Once Epiphanius was passing through a place where all the rich men were sitting on their chairs. Draco the Great and his sick son were there too. When they saw Epiphanius, they mocked him. But Epiphanius came up to them, bowed to them, and took young Draco by the hand, saying, “Draco, you too, be well.” And at once, at Epiphanius’s word, Draco was healed.

Everyone who saw it was astonished. When the elder Draco saw what Epiphanius had done, he was so seized with fear and trembling that he could no longer walk about his house on his own feet as he used to; they had to carry him and lay him on a bed. At dawn Draco’s wife came and begged Epiphanius to come and pray and raise him up. So Epiphanius went to Draco’s house, and when he had prayed, Draco rose from his bed at once. The next morning Draco took five thousand gold coins and brought them to Epiphanius. But Epiphanius said, “For me, child, one little tunic for this poor body is enough, and coarse bread with water to drink. Why do you bring me a burden, when I do not want you to be burdened either? If you wish to be glorified, go and devote yourself to the house of God, and give these to the sick and the toiling.” Draco did so, and he entreated Epiphanius, who baptised him and his wife. 42. There was another man named Synesius, also rich, who was a pagan. He had an only son, thirteen years old. A disease came upon the boy, closed around his throat and choked him, and he died, and there was mourning and lamentation in the house. A certain Hermias, a Christian, said to the boy’s mother, “Lady, beg the great Epiphanius to come, and he would raise the boy.” She believed, and at once sent Hermias to Epiphanius, for Hermias was close to him. Hermias came and said to Epiphanius, “Lord, my master Synesius has sent me to you to bring you to his house, so that you may pray to God for his son, who has died, that he may rise.” Then Epiphanius took me, and we went to the house of Synesius. When Epiphanius entered the house, Synesius’s wife fell to the ground and spoke to Epiphanius in these words: “You have come here, great physician of the Christians. Show us your skill; let us see it, let us put it to the test (a) by being healed, and so let us come over to your Christ.” When the woman had said this, Epiphanius said to her, “If you believe in the Crucified, you will see the boy walking.” The woman said, “There is nothing else in my mind but only to hold to the Crucified.” Then Epiphanius went up to the bed, touched the boy’s throat, rubbed his neck, and said to him with a cheerful face, “Eustorgius.” At once the boy opened his eyes and sat up on the bed, and everyone in the house was amazed. When Eustorgius’s mother saw what had been done for the child through Epiphanius, she took three thousand gold coins and brought them to Epiphanius. But Epiphanius said to her, “I have no use for these, good lady. Let your husband Synesius take them and go to the house of the one who raised your son, and give them to those who toil.” Synesius did (a) [?] read ἴδωμεν, λάβωμεν, as the following προσέλθωμεν [?].
so. He was baptised, along with his wife and his son, whom [?] had raised from the dead…

43. Once, when we were in the house with no one else present, Epiphanius said to me, “Polybius, my child, since the Church needs a presbyter in place of our father John, I want you, my child, to take his rank.” I took his words hard and declined with a great many excuses, but then the time for church came, to do the work of the Lord. As we were all going into the church with Epiphanius, I thought of running away, since I considered the burden of the presbyterate too heavy. When he reached the sanctuary, Epiphanius took me by the hand and said to me, “Stay here until it is time.” All who heard this were amazed. And I could no longer lift my foot from the spot; I was as if nailed down with iron. When the whole service was finished, he sent one of the deacons, who brought me to the altar, and he ordained me presbyter. After the dismissal of the congregation, I fell ill from fear and was confined to my bed until Epiphanius came and prayed, and at once I got up. 44. At that time a deacon came from Jerusalem and told Epiphanius about John, the bishop of Jerusalem: that he was a lover of money, who locked up his wealth and gave nothing to the needy. This John had lived in the monastery of the great Hilarion, while Epiphanius was living there with him. So Epiphanius wrote John a letter about showing mercy to those in need, but John did nothing about the letter. Not long afterwards Epiphanius said to me, “Come, child, let us go to Jerusalem, worship there, and come back.” We set out from Cyprus and sailed to Caesarea of Philip, and from there we went up to Jerusalem. When we had arrived and prayed, we went up to the bishop’s residence. John saw Epiphanius and was overjoyed. Epiphanius said to John, “Give me a house to stay in, my child.” He gave us a very fine house. Every day John invited Epiphanius to his table and served us lavish food and drink, while the poor received no share even of this. One day Epiphanius said to John, “Father John, lend me some silver plate for serving, for I have some Cypriot men to entertain, and I will impress them with your silver. Provide your servant with the finest things in your house, to your own glory, and I will boast of your generosity. Just keep a record of what you give, and afterwards I will return what is due.” So John brought out a great deal of silver before Epiphanius. Epiphanius said to John, “Do you have still more stored away

…silver, Father?” [?] John said to Epiphanius, “This is enough for your service for now, Father.” Epiphanius said to John, “Bring that other one too, Father, so that we may entertain guests.” When John had brought the rest as well, Epiphanius said to him, “Give me the things that dazzle free men.” John said to Epiphanius, “Take everything that will delight your people, and serve them at the meal.”

45. Epiphanius took a weight of silver of about fifteen hundred pounds, and we went to the house John had given us to stay in. There was a silver dealer named Asterius, who had come from Rome to Jerusalem on business. Epiphanius summoned him, showed him the silver, came to terms with him and closed the deal, and sold it to him, receiving gold in return. Once he had the gold, Epiphanius gave it out night and day to those in need. Some days later John said to Epiphanius, “Give me back the silver I lent you for your service.” Epiphanius said to John, “Be patient with me, child, for I have people to feed, and I will repay everything.” After some more days had passed, while we were standing in the church where the saving wood is kept, John said to Epiphanius, “I have told you already: give me back the silver I lent you.” Epiphanius answered John quietly, “I told you, Father, that I will repay you.” Then John, filled with great anger, seized Epiphanius by his cloak and held on to it, twisting it tight around him, and said to him, “You shall not leave, you shall not sit down, you shall have no peace until you give back the silver you borrowed from me, [?] Epiphanius. Give back to the Church what belongs to the Church.” Through all this Epiphanius was not troubled, but remained just as composed as before. John went on holding him and insulting him for two hours. All the bystanders grew weary of standing there and listening to John’s harsh words. Then Epiphanius, not in the least distressed, breathed into John’s face, and at once John was blinded, and fear fell on all who stood by. John fell on his face before Epiphanius, begging him to pray that he might see again. Epiphanius said, “Go and venerate the precious cross, and it will grant you this.” But John kept on entreating Epiphanius. So Epiphanius instructed him and laid his hand on him, and his right eye was opened. John then begged for the left as well. Epiphanius said to John, “This is not mine to do, child. God closed it, and God opened it; he has done as he willed, so that we might learn sense.” And John, chastened and rebuked by a righteous man, became [?] in all things.

46. As we were leaving the city to sail to Cyprus, there were two jesters at a certain spot. As Epiphanius was passing that spot, [?]

one of them said to him, “Holy Father Epiphanius, look upon this dead man and throw your covering over him.” When Epiphanius heard this, he stood facing east and offered a prayer for the dead man; then he took off his outer garment and threw it over the dead man to clothe him. As Epiphanius went on his way, the one who had spoken said to the man pretending to be dead, “Get up, the simpleton has gone past.” When he gave no answer, he called him again. When he saw that he was dead, he said to himself, “Let me run and tell the stranger what happened, so that he may raise him.” He ran after us, fell to the ground and pleaded with Epiphanius, saying, “I beg and beseech your fatherhood: help us, and pardon our folly. When I called to you, ‘Clothe the dead man,’ I spoke those words by arrangement with him; and when you had passed us, Father, not far off, I spoke to my companion, and there was no voice and no one listening.
