But come, Father, raise the dead man, and take back the tunic we received from you.” Epiphanius said to the man, “Go, child, and bury him; for he died first, and only then did you ask for the garment.” We went down again to Caesarea and sailed to Cyprus, and the brothers welcomed us with great joy.

47. There was a Jewish teacher of the law named Isaac, a devout man who kept the law of Moses strictly. He attached himself to Epiphanius, was instructed by him, and was baptized. So the three of us lived together in one house.

48. Once the sister of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, who was suffering from an illness (she was living in Rome), heard that God was healing the sick through Epiphanius. So she sent to Cyprus to bring Epiphanius to Rome. When the envoys reached Cyprus, they presented the letters at the bishop’s residence. Now there was a wealthy pagan, who stammered badly, named Faustinianus. He welcomed the men who had been sent to Epiphanius; he was also bitterly hostile to Epiphanius. Faustinianus said to them, “Why do you heed this impostor as if he were a god? He speaks empty words, and nothing else [?] suffered.” And Faustinianus fell on his face and lay there dead. Epiphanius came over to Faustinianus, took him by the hand and said, “Rise, child, in the name of the Lord, and go home in good health.” At once Faustinianus

got up and went to his house. When his wife heard what had happened, she took a thousand gold coins and brought them to Epiphanius. Epiphanius said to the woman, “Go, child, give them to those who labor in the church, and you will have treasure with the Most High.” And the woman did so.

49. The envoys sent by the emperors pressed Epiphanius to sail to Rome. Now there was a cleric named Philo, formerly a rhetorician, a holy man. The city of Carpasia needed a bishop to be seated on its throne, and Philo was a deacon. By a revelation from God, Epiphanius ordained him bishop of the throne of the city and church of Carpasia. So when Epiphanius was about to go to Rome, he sent for this bishop Philo and entrusted him with authority over the church of Constantia, so that if clergy were needed he could ordain them. Then Epiphanius took me and Isaac, and we sailed to Rome. When we entered the city, there was mourning and great lamentation in the imperial apartments. The sister of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius had an illness in her right hand, and the physicians had tried many things without helping her at all. By now the disease was eating away her flesh. In her great distress she was urging the emperors, Arcadius and Honorius, to allow a physician to give her poison, so that she might quickly be done with this life. Those who had brought us to Rome went in and reported to the emperors, and they gave leave for Epiphanius to enter. Epiphanius, though he was not used to meeting such people, went into the imperial apartments quite fearlessly and approached the emperors. Their sister was lying on her bed.

50. When the emperors saw Epiphanius, they at once rose from their thrones. Epiphanius said to the emperors, “Give this honor, children, to the Benefactor, and you will see your sister in the best of health. Do not trust in power, children, and you will be guarded by the Lord.” At Epiphanius’s words the emperors hesitated and were troubled. Epiphanius said to them, “Why do you hesitate at what is being said, children? Through what is being said you will see the grace of God.” Then Epiphanius went to the bed where the emperors’ sister lay and said to her with a kindly face, “Do not doubt, child, because of your illness. Set your hope on the living God, and you will see health this very hour. Believe in the crucified Son of God, and you will be walking this very hour. The pain of your body, child, has ceased. Glorify God who gives this grace; keep him in your mind without ceasing, and he will be a wall around you for all time.” With these words Epiphanius took her hand and signed her with the cross three times, and at once she was relieved of her pains. When the emperors saw what Epiphanius had done, their hearts were drawn to love him,

to listen to him, and to believe everything he said; and they begged him to stay with them in Rome and to be a father to them. Every day Epiphanius taught them and strengthened them.

51. Now their sister, who had had the illness and been healed by Epiphanius, had a son; and it happened that, without having been ill, he was found dead on his bed, so that there was great mourning in the palace. The emperors said to Epiphanius, “Pray for the child, Father, so that you may give him back alive to his mother.” Epiphanius said, “And do you believe that I can do this?” The emperors said to him, “We believe that just as you drove the illness out of the child’s mother, so you will present the child alive to his mother.” Epiphanius said to them, “If your sister’s son rises, will you believe and be baptized in the name of the Crucified?” The emperors said, “If you raise the boy, we will believe and be baptized.” So Epiphanius went to the child’s bed, signed his whole body with the cross, prayed to the one who puts to death and brings to life, and said to the boy, “Rise, child, in the name of Jesus Christ the crucified.” And at once the boy sat up on his bed. Then the emperors, believing that Epiphanius had raised the boy through prayer, begged him to baptize them. Epiphanius said to them, “I welcome your piety in every way, for it is God who is stirring you to this. But I cannot do it without the permission of the bishop of Rome, lest he be offended with me.” So the emperors at once sent for the bishop of the church of the Romans and told him everything. The bishop rejoiced greatly when he heard this from the emperors, and gave Epiphanius permission to baptize them.

52. When they entered the baptistery to be baptized by Epiphanius, and the whole order of service had been carried out, Arcadius went in first and looked, and behold, three men wearing white robes were attending Epiphanius, one on his right and one on his left, and the third following behind him. And he was seized with great fear. Epiphanius knew from Arcadius’s face that he had seen a vision, and said to him, “Take heed to yourself, child, and be on your guard.” It was Epiphanius’s custom not to put anyone into the font until the water had been stirred. After Arcadius had been baptized, he brought in Honorius too, and he saw the same vision. Then their sister’s son went down, and their sister herself, Procliana, who was the wife of one of the patricians. After they had been baptized, Epiphanius spent the seven days with them, teaching them. And after they had taken off their white baptismal garments, Epiphanius said to the two emperors, “Stand firm, children. The wolf shall no longer have dominion over you; pain and sorrow and sighing have fled away. Keep your minds on the resurrection, and do not grieve

over those who depart from this life; for those who have believed in Christ have put on Christ and have him as their helper. For,” he said, “the child who once died and rose again, having received grace, is about to depart to the Savior, and you will see him in great glory, escorted by angels.” The next morning, while Epiphanius was in the imperial apartments teaching the emperors, a sweet fragrance spread among us all. Epiphanius said to the emperors, “Stand up and pray, sons of light.” The child was lying on his bed; and when Epiphanius had said the prayer, everyone in the imperial apartments heard what sounded like a great crowd saying the Amen, and at once the boy gave up his spirit. We stayed in Rome a whole year, and Epiphanius worked many other signs there. When Epiphanius decided that we should sail back to Cyprus, the emperors said to him, “Take, Father, what the Church needs, so that you can provide for those in want.” Epiphanius said to them, “You, children, do what is asked of you; I rejoice at your generosity. But do not lay a burden on me. For my God provides all things for all, nourishing everyone in this life.” The emperors brought a great deal of gold, but Epiphanius accepted none of it; he only asked them to send a few loaves for us to eat on the ship. So we set out from Rome and arrived in Cyprus after forty days, and the brothers welcomed us with great joy.

53. It was Epiphanius’s custom to go out at night to the cemeteries where the relics of the holy martyrs lie, and to plead with God for each one of the afflicted. And just as a friend who asks a friend obtains what he asks for, so God granted him his requests. Once, when there was a great famine and no bread could be found in the market, Faustinianus the merciless had many storehouses full of wheat and barley locked up tight. He would take gold and give each needy person three modii for a gold coin, and there was great hardship in the city. Epiphanius said to Faustinianus, “My good man, give me wheat to feed the people, and I will repay you what is owed for all of it.” But the merciless Faustinianus began to talk to Epiphanius like this: “Go and plead with the God you worship, and he will give you wheat to feed your friends.” So one night Epiphanius went out to the cemeteries and pleaded with God to feed all those in distress. Now there was an ancient temple called the Safety of Zeus; and if anyone ever came near this temple, it was said that death seized him at once. While Epiphanius was praying to God for the afflicted, a voice came to him: “Epiphanius, do not be troubled.” He said, “What [?]

(a) Patristic edition: “The child who once died and rose again, having received grace … and you will see.”

is it, Lord?” And the voice said to him, “Go to the temple called the Safety of Zeus, and the seals on its doors will be loosed; go in, and you will find a great deal of gold. Take it, buy all of Faustinianus’s wheat and barley, and give food to those in need.” So Epiphanius went to the temple, and as he approached its entrance, the seals at once fell off and the doors opened; Epiphanius went in and found a great deal of gold. He took it and paid Faustinianus out of it, saying, “Take this money and give me wheat.” The money-loving, accursed Faustinianus accepted the gold and supplied him with wheat at three modii a coin. Epiphanius gave wheat to everyone in need, and the money did not run out until he had bought up all the food Faustinianus had amassed. Epiphanius filled many storehouses with the wheat and barley bought from Faustinianus and supplied the whole city — or rather, God did so through Epiphanius.

54. So there was plenty for everyone, and great hardship in the house of Faustinianus. The wicked and violent Faustinianus, now in straits because of his love of money, and thinking it beneath him to ask Epiphanius for food for his household, hired five more ships in addition to his own, gave money to Longinus, his most trusted servant, and sent him to Calabria to buy wheat there to feed his household. The ships sailed out and were loaded with wheat and other goods, and after four months they were sailing back with the wheat, a hundred stades from Constantia, opposite the place called Dianeuterion. A great storm arose on the sea, and all of Faustinianus’s ships carrying the wheat were in danger, and the sea cast all the wheat up on the shore. When Faustinianus heard this, he went down to the sea at once, and when he saw with his own eyes what had happened, the wretch, his mouth an open grave, immediately began to blaspheme the Most High and to heap insults like these on Epiphanius: “Look, this sorcerer and impostor works evil against my house not only on dry land but on the sea as well, sending demons to stop what was meant to supply my household from getting in. Oh, what wind blew this impostor here?” After saying this and more, he went home, uttering threats against Epiphanius. Then all the men and women of the city gathered, together with their children, collected the wheat and carried it off to their homes, laying in their own supply, some enough for a year, some for two. Now the wretched Faustinianus had a wife who did good works. Without her husband’s knowledge she sent two thousand gold coins to Epiphanius, so that he would provide food for her household. Epiphanius said to the woman, “Keep the coins in your house,

and take provisions for your household; and when the land yields its harvest, then you can repay what you have received.” And he did this for the woman.

55. There was a deacon at the bishop’s residence named Sabinus, a calligrapher by profession. He was gentle and adorned with an upright life. There were eighty of us monks in all at the bishop’s residence, and this Sabinus stood out among us all. Epiphanius appointed him to judge the Church’s cases. Once two men brought a case before Sabinus, one rich and one poor, and the rich man had the better claim. Epiphanius, standing in a hidden spot and listening to the case, heard Sabinus showing pity instead and leaning toward the poor man in his judgment. So Epiphanius came out into the middle and said to Sabinus with a kindly face, “Go, child, do your calligraphy; and keeping the divine Scriptures in mind, be perfect in judgment. Listen to the Benefactor, who calls out and says, ‘You shall not pity the poor in judgment, nor show favor to the powerful.’” From then on Epiphanius himself judged everyone who came. From morning until the ninth hour he heard the litigants, and from the ninth hour until morning no one saw him.

56. There was one of the brothers at the bishop’s residence, a brazen-faced man, who was also a calligrapher by trade; his name was Rufinus. He fell in with Faustinianus and every day heaped many insults on Epiphanius, while Epiphanius with great gentleness restrained his insolence. At Faustinianus’s instigation, and through the working of the demon that was at work in them, he sought to kill Epiphanius. Faustinianus had made an agreement with the monk, the wretch telling him, “If you kill this impostor, you will sit on the throne.” This Rufinus was the lowest-ranking deacon of the church, and so it was his custom to make the bishop’s throne ready. So this bold and arrogant man took a sharp knife and set it upright on the seat of the throne, with the throne’s cover spread over it. When Epiphanius was about to sit on the throne, he said to the man who had laid the trap, “Child, take the cover off the throne.” When he did not obey Epiphanius’s word, Epiphanius took the cloth that was hiding the knife himself, and the knife fell at the feet of Rufinus the deacon and stuck fast in his right foot. Epiphanius said to Rufinus, “Stop your unruliness, child, lest you come to harm before long. Leave the church, then, for you are not worthy to partake of the divine mysteries.” Rufinus left the church and went to the bishop’s residence, lay down on his bed, and three days later ended his life.

57. At that time the emperor Theodosius, having taken offense — on what pretext I do not know —

…his feet; from the knees down that whole part of his body was paralysed, and he had been lying in bed for seven months. He sent to Epiphanius in Cyprus, asking him to come up to the imperial city of Constantinople to help him in his suffering. When the men the emperor had sent arrived, the grief and tears of the brethren kept Epiphanius from leaving Cyprus, for whenever he sailed away from Cyprus, all the brethren prayed for death. But when the emperor's envoys pressed Epiphanius to come up to the imperial city, Epiphanius said to them, “Go to the emperor, children, and I will follow after you.” They replied, “Do not be angry, Father, but this is the emperor's command, and we cannot do otherwise, or we may be in danger, especially since the emperor is ill and waiting for word from you, Father.” With difficulty they persuaded Epiphanius to sail with them. So Epiphanius sent for the most God-loving bishop Philo and entrusted to him the care of the church's affairs. Then all the fathers and brethren gathered and received instruction from Epiphanius; we embraced them all and sailed for the imperial city. When we entered Constantinople, Epiphanius's arrival was announced to the emperor. The emperor ordered us to come into the palace, and Epiphanius went in with great dignity. The emperor Theodosius II was lying in bed, unable to speak for the pain. When Epiphanius came near him, the emperor said to Epiphanius, “Pray for me, Father, that I may be well.” Epiphanius said to the emperor, “Believe, child, in the one who was crucified, and you will have health without ceasing. Keep God in your mind, and no evil will master you. Be merciful to the afflicted, and you will receive mercy from God. As emperor, honour the one who gave you your power, and he will give you greater grace.” Having said this to the emperor, Epiphanius came close, touched his feet, and sealed him with the sign of the cross three times. Then Epiphanius said to the emperor, “Get up from your bed, child, for the pain has left your feet.” Hearing this, the emperor at once rose from his bed, with nothing wrong with his feet. The emperor said to Epiphanius, “Father, give me your commands always, and I will satisfy you in everything.” Epiphanius said to the emperor, “Keep God's words in your soul, and you will have no need of Epiphanius.” When Epiphanius had said this and more to the emperor, it was time for the midday meal. Epiphanius said to the emperor, “Go to table, child, and bless your benefactor.” For Epiphanius was gracious and urbane, and his speech was seasoned with divine salt. Now when the daughter of Theodosius, the sister of Arcadius and Honorius, fell ill in Rome, they too went to Rome and spent five years with her, because she had been married there.

So when the emperor Theodosius heard that Epiphanius had gone to Rome and healed his daughter, and had also raised her son to life when he was dead, and had enlightened Arcadius and Honorius as well, he rejoiced with great joy. From then on he wrote to him as to a father. While we were in Constantinople, Arcadius and Honorius arrived from Rome, and they rejoiced with great joy.

58. By the emperor's order some men brought Faustinian from Cyprus to the imperial city, accused of slandering the emperor, and he was kept under guard at the emperor's command. When Epiphanius heard this, he went to the place where Faustinian was held and said to him, “Child, if you wish to send a word to the emperor through us, you will be released from this confinement.” Faustinian said to Epiphanius, “Go away, deceiver, and lead astray unstable men; do not speak such words to Faustinian. You came here to gloat over me with words. From now on keep away from Cyprus. Go to Phoenicia and busy yourself with mischief forever.” When Faustinian had insulted Epiphanius in this way, Epiphanius took me with him, and we went to the palace to take leave of the emperor and sail for Cyprus. But the emperor begged Epiphanius to stay a few days in the imperial city, and Epiphanius explained the reason for his departure. Again the emperor won Epiphanius over with his words. The next morning one of the messengers came into the palace with the news that Faustinian the Cypriot had died. Hearing this, Epiphanius mourned for Faustinian. The emperor wanted to transfer all of Faustinian's property to the imperial treasury, especially since he had left no offspring on earth. But Epiphanius said to the emperor, “Take care, child, that you do not commit a sin. For Faustinian has a wife who fears God with all her heart. Listen to Epiphanius's words, and you will have favour from the Most High.” Then the emperor gave Epiphanius full authority over Faustinian's estate. Epiphanius said to the emperor, “I have God, child, who supplies my needs, and with the wife's consent we will give all of this to those in need.” When Epiphanius had said this, the emperor said, “Ask for whatever you need, Father, and I will give it willingly.” Epiphanius said to the emperor, “Keep my words always, and keep me, child, in your soul.” When Epiphanius had said this, the emperor came out of the palace with us and begged Epiphanius to bless him. Epiphanius said a prayer, blessed the emperor and embraced him, and the emperor returned to his palace in peace. Nine days later we sailed to Cyprus, and the brethren welcomed us with great joy. We found Faustinian's wife mourning for her husband. Epiphanius comforted her in all her grief, and she was won over by his words and begged Epiphanius to give her the seal in Christ. He baptized her and ordained

her a deaconess of the church, and all her possessions were given to those in need as Epiphanius judged best.

59. Once Epiphanius debated with Aetius, the bishop of the Valentinians, for there were crowds of this heresy in Constantia. Aetius argued contentiously at great length and came to utter many blasphemies against the Most High, and Epiphanius said to him, “Most impious Aetius, take a gag upon your mouth, and speak no more disorderly words.” At Epiphanius's word Aetius was instantly struck dumb, and from that day he could no longer speak a word. When the members of his heresy saw that he had silenced him with a word, they all fell down before Epiphanius, anathematized their own religion, and became orthodox. Aetius remained without speech for six days, and on the seventh day he died. There were also other [?] heresies in the land of Cyprus, namely these: the Sophists, the Sabellians, the Nicolaitans, the Simonians, the Basilidians and the Carpocratians. About these Epiphanius wrote a letter to the emperor Theodosius, asking him to drive them from the island by imperial decree. For there were rich men among them, who were even entrusted with public offices and oppressed the orthodox. When the emperor received the letter from Epiphanius, he issued a decree to this effect: “If anyone does not obey the divine teaching of Father Epiphanius, bishop of the land of Cyprus, let him leave the island and live wherever he wishes. But if there are any who are friends and children of repentance, and who confess to our common Father, ‘We have gone astray and wish to come to the way of truth,’ let them remain on the island and be taught by our common Father.” When the decree arrived by the hand of an official and was published, many of them were persuaded by Epiphanius. Those who were not persuaded were at once driven from the island.

60. There was a bishop in Alexandria named Theophilus, who was well acquainted with Epiphanius. There were also three brothers in Alexandria, sons of Heracleon, who had been governor of that city. After their father died, the three agreed together to become monks. So they went into the desert, where they lived in deep stillness, adorned with a fitting way of life. They were well known to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. Theophilus brought them into the city by deceit and kept them there. He made the eldest of them bishop of a city in Egypt and made the others deacons and stewards of the church. After they had managed the church for three years, the two felt that they were growing dead to divine grace, since they had left their stillness, and they agreed together to beg Theophilus to release them to the place where they had lived before. When he did not yield to their request, the two, of one mind again, withdrew and went away

into the desert where they had lived before. So Theophilus [?] barred them from the assembly and from communion for three years. They pleaded with him many times to be allowed to partake of the divine mysteries, but Theophilus would not allow it. Forced by this, they went up to the imperial city and fell at the feet of John, surnamed Chrysostom. When John learned the reason, he wrote a letter to Theophilus, asking him to release the two brothers. Theophilus did not heed John's request; John wrote a second time to plead with Theophilus, and even so he did not heed John. Then John released the two brothers from the excommunication, and as a result great bitterness arose between Theophilus and John.

61. At that time there was a senator named Theognostus. He was a Christian who always kept the fear of God, and he was loved by the emperor. There was another man, also of the senate, called Dorotheus, who was an Arian. He accused Theognostus of insulting the emperor; he brought forward two false witnesses and confronted Theognostus to his face. So the emperor Theodosius ordered Theognostus to be exiled and his property confiscated. Theognostus's wife was left with one suburban estate, from which she made her living. Theognostus died on his way into exile. Once, at the time of the grape harvest, the empress Eudoxia went out in procession to the place where the estate of Theognostus's wife was, and for what reason I do not know, the empress went into the woman's vineyard and cut off a cluster of grapes. Some of those attending the empress said to her, “Lady, the vineyard where you cut the cluster belongs to someone else.” Now it is the custom with emperors and empresses that if they so much as set foot on another's property, or take fruit from any fruit-bearing tree, no one else has ownership of it any longer, but only the emperor. When Theognostus's wife heard that her field had been taken from her, she wrote on a tablet and sent it to John, for he was greatly loved by the emperor and the empress. When John learned of this, he sent his archdeacon, an eloquent man adorned with an upright life, whose name was Eutychus. Eutychus went in to the empress and spoke with her as John had instructed. The empress said to Eutychus, “This is the law. But wherever she wishes, in another province, I will give her a property.” Eutychus went out and reported the empress's words to John. John went to the palace and said to the empress, “Give back the widow's field.” The empress said to John, “Learn the reason, Father, and then bring the charge of wrongdoing that you say I committed against the widow.” And again the empress said to John, “Do not be eager to rebuke emperors to their faces.” John said, “And again I say to you: give back the widow's field. You have heard how Jezebel is held up to shame, and to this day is pointed out by divine Scripture for her wickedness, because of the vineyard of a holy man.”

When the empress heard this from John, she ordered him to be thrown out of the palace. So he went out and went to the church. John said to Eutychus, “When the empress comes to the church, take the attendants with you and stand at the entrance where she usually comes in, and do not let her enter. Say that John has ordered that she is not to enter the church.” And Eutychus did so. From then on the empress was stirred up against John, to have him banished.

62. When Theophilus heard that the empress wanted to banish John, he too schemed against him all the more. So Theophilus wrote Epiphanius a great many letters against John, saying that John held the views of Origen. And the empress was stirred up to banish him. Epiphanius was persuaded by Theophilus on this point, not knowing that Theophilus bore hostility toward John. It happened that Epiphanius wanted to sail to the imperial city on urgent business. Having heard such things about John from Theophilus, he hastened all the more to go up, not to harm John but to help him. So he took me and Isaac, and we sailed to Constantinople. When we entered the city, there was great turmoil over John, because John was much loved by the citizens. There were certain monasteries and martyrs' shrines that received allowances from the empress and would not accept John. When we went into one of these monasteries, they pressed Epiphanius to ordain someone, since there was need, for the service of the church. He did so, and when John heard of it he was deeply offended with Epiphanius and wrote Epiphanius a letter that caused hurt. Epiphanius replied to John in the same vein about what he had written. The empress heard that John was offended with Epiphanius, and she summoned Epiphanius and said to him, “Father Epiphanius, the whole empire of the Romans is mine, and the whole priesthood of the churches under my rule is yours. Since John, a stranger to the good order of the priesthood, behaves disorderly toward emperors, and they say he holds some heresy, my mind has been troubled for many days about holding a synod, having him deposed from the priesthood as unworthy, and seating on the throne someone else who is able to uphold the priesthood, so that my reign may have peace in all things.” As the empress said this to Epiphanius, she was all agitated with great anger. Again she said to him, “Since your paternity is here, after God, there is no need to put the other fathers to trouble. Whomever God reveals to you, make him bishop, and throw this man out of the church.” Epiphanius said to the empress, “Listen patiently, child, to your father.” The empress said to

Epiphanius, “If your paternity commands anything, tell me, and I will serve my father.” Epiphanius said to the empress, “If John is condemned for the heresy you speak of, and is proved guilty, and does not confess that he has sinned, he is unworthy of the priesthood, and I will do whatever your authority commands. But if you are seeking to drive John from the church because of the insult to you, your Epiphanius will not consent to it. Above all, child, it is for emperors to be insulted and to forgive. For you too have a King in heaven against whom you habitually sin, and he forgives you if you forgive those who insult you. As he says in the Gospels: ‘Be merciful, as your Father in heaven is.’” The empress said to Epiphanius, “If you stand in the way of John's banishment, Father Epiphanius, I will open the temples of the idols and make people worship them, and I will make the last things worse than the first.” As she said this bitterly, tears poured from her eyes. Epiphanius said, “I, child, am innocent of this judgment.”

63. Having said this, Epiphanius took me with him and we left the palace. Isaac was ill and had not gone in with us to the empress. A rumour ran through the whole city, people saying, “The great priest Epiphanius, the bishop of Cyprus, went in to the empress and brought about the banishment of the great John.” When Isaac heard this too, he ran away from Epiphanius, went into a monastery and stayed there without our knowing. Epiphanius grieved over him as well and prayed to God to make known to him where Isaac was staying. God made it known to him, and we went to him. Isaac turned away from Epiphanius, saying, “I no longer wish to be with you, because of the sin you committed against John.” We spent three days in the monastery, and with difficulty he persuaded Isaac; we took him and left. John too was convinced that Epiphanius had consented to his banishment. He took a tablet and wrote to Epiphanius: “Wise Epiphanius, you have consented to my banishment. You will never again sit on your throne.” Epiphanius in turn wrote back to John: “Athlete, be beaten and win. Because you believed that I consented to your banishment, you will never reach the place to which you have been banished.” I have written this, brothers, so that no one may cast blame on Epiphanius in this matter. Could the man who had accomplished so much good have sunk to such a depth of evil? God forbid! When we went into the palace, Epiphanius took leave of the emperors so that we could sail for Cyprus. When Epiphanius was asked by the emperor Arcadius how old he was, he said, “I am a hundred and five years old, less three months. Thus,” he said, “I was sixty years old when I (a) Perhaps “thus.” [?] Patrol. Gr. XLI.

became bishop, and I have been in the episcopate fifty-five years less three months.” He asked him this on the very day we were to board the ship. When we had boarded the ship, Epiphanius sat down in the hold of the ship, and we with him. It was Epiphanius's custom always to hold the holy Gospels in his hands. Three times he groaned and wept; he opened the holy Gospels, closed them again and wept, and said a prayer. After the prayer he sat down in the hold of the ship and began to weep and say to us:

64. “If you love me, children, keep my commandments, and the love of God will remain in you. You know through how many afflictions I have passed in this life, and I counted none of them an affliction, but I was always rejoicing, looking to God, and God did not forsake me; he himself guarded me from every scheme of the evil one. For all things work together for good for those who love God. Once, my dearly beloved children, when I was in a desert place offering my prayer to Christ to be delivered from every scheme of the adversary, a crowd of demons came upon me, threw me to the ground, seized me by the feet and dragged me along the ground. Some of them also beat me. They did this to me for ten days. From then on I never again saw a demon face to face all the days of my life; instead they carried out their malice against me through wicked men. What evils befell me in Phoenicia from the disorderly Simonians, in Egypt from the unclean Gnostics, and in Cyprus from the lawless Valentinians and the other heresies! Pay attention, children, and hear the word of Epiphanius the sinner. Do not be lovers of money, and much money will be added to you. Do not hate anyone, and you will be loved by God. Do not slander a brother, and no devilish passion will master you. Turn away from all heresies as from beasts with deadly venom; I have also handed down to you in writing about them in the books called the Panarion. Turn away from and guard yourselves against the pleasure of the world, which always tickles the body and the mind. You know from experience that it is an instrument of Satan. For often, even when the flesh is at rest, the minds of the unguarded fantasize about shameful things. But when our mind is sober and always keeps God in remembrance, we can easily overthrow the enemy.” Having said this and more, Epiphanius called together everyone on the ship and said to them, “Brothers, we must pray with all our strength to God, the lover of mankind, that he may save us and that no one on the ship may perish. For a great storm is about to arise. But take heart:

for no affliction will touch anyone on the ship." After saying this, he said to me, "Polybius, my child." I said to him, "What is it, Father?" He said to me, "When we have sailed back to Constantia, spend seven days in the city, then sail to Egypt, go up into the Upper Thebaid, and shepherd the sheep of Christ. But watch yourself, child. I call heaven and earth to witness against you: do not do otherwise. For if you twist my words and do not go, you will utterly perish, all that you have built will come to nothing for you, and you will be worthless in the sight of all people. But if you listen to my words and keep the commandment of the Lord which Jesus Christ, the Son of God, gave me, you will be blessed before him all your days." After saying this to me, he embraced me. Then he turned to Isaac and said to him, "Child."

65. He said, "What is it, Father?" And Epiphanius said, "You too, child, remain in Constantia until you are permitted to walk the way of the (a) righteous." After saying this to Isaac, Epiphanius embraced him too. Then he called all the sailors together and said to them, "Do not be alarmed, children. The sea is going to be very rough. But pray to God, and he will help you." It was the eleventh hour of the day when Epiphanius taught us these things. And he said to one of the sailors, "Do not tempt, lest you be tempted." About sunset a great squall arose on the sea. Epiphanius was in the hold of the ship with his hands stretched out, the Gospels lying on his breast, his eyes open, and his voice could not be heard. All of us, gripped by great fear, supposed that Epiphanius was praying to God because of the tossing of the sea. The storm lasted two days and two nights. On the third day Epiphanius said to me, "Polybius, my child, speak to the sailors and have them light wood and make a charcoal fire. And take incense and bring it here." I did so and brought it to him. He said to me, "Put the incense on the fire." And I put it on. And he said, "Pray, children." And he offered a prayer as was customary. After the prayer he embraced us and said, "Farewell, children, for Epiphanius will see you no more in this life." And at once he gave up his spirit, and immediately the storm on the sea ceased. 66. Isaac and I fell on his neck and wept bitterly, and darkness fell upon our eyes in that hour. Now one of the sailors, the one to whom Epiphanius had said while still alive, "Do not tempt, lest you be tempted," ran to Epiphanius's feet and wanted to lift his garment to see whether he was circumcised. But Epiphanius, lying there dead as he was, raised his right foot and struck him in the face, and hurled him from the hold of the ship to the stern, and he lay dead. He remained lying dead for two days. On the (a) The translator read "of the Citians."

third day, then, the sailors lifted him up and carried him close to Epiphanius. When they laid him at his feet, he touched his feet and at once rose up, and fear fell on everyone on the ship. When we had put in at Constantia at the place called Dianeuterion, the sailors left the ship, went all around the city, and cried out with loud voices: "Brothers, you who live in the populous metropolis of Constantia, come down to the sea at the place called Dianeuterion and receive the precious remains of our holy father Epiphanius, for he has ended this human life." Then darkness fell on the whole city, and they came down to the sea leading one another by the hand, making great lamentation. The whole countryside, too, streamed into the city, shedding tears along the road; so much so that when three blind men from the parish called Stortyke had set out on the road, no one would give them a hand so that they might reach the city more quickly. Then one of the three, named Prosechius, said, "Saint of God, holy Epiphanius, make us see again, so that we too may venerate your precious remains." And at once they recovered their sight, and entering the city they venerated the precious remains of the holy father, and told what had happened to them on the road. When everyone heard it, they glorified God, who grants such things to those who are worthy of him. 67. They took the remains from the ship and carried them with great honor into the church. He lay there three days and was not buried, because of their great contention. On the fourth day, then, having laid [?], they placed him in Skyrion (a) [?]. I myself spent the seven days in the church beside the remains, and even so he had not been buried. On the eighth day, then, in accordance with the (b) of the holy father, I found a ship crossing to Egypt, went on board and sailed, went up into the Upper Thebaid, and spent a year there. Then the great Heraclion, the governor of Egypt, coming down to the city of Rhinocorura (for he was a resident of it), heard that I had been a disciple of the great Epiphanius; and against my will he had me seized by soldiers, set me on a racing camel, and brought me down to Rhinocorura. It happened that the bishop there had died, and he had me ordained bishop of the church of Rhinocorura. Letter of Polybius, bishop of the city of Rhinocorura, to Sabinus, bishop of Constantia. To the God-honored lord, worthy of the priesthood, the holy father Bishop Sabinus of the city of Constantia in Cyprus, Polybius, a sinner, greeting in the Lord. The Magi shared in grace — I mean even before the star revealed to them that they should make the journey to Jerusalem, and to Bethlehem, to worship the great King, Jesus Christ our Lord. For if they had not had knowledge of God beforehand, (b) According to the [?] command. The same.

they would not have attained the vision of God. But they (a) inquired about God, who was sought by the Magi and made known by the star to those same Magi in Bethlehem; whereas I am inquiring about a holy man who served the God who was sought by the Magi and found and worshiped at Bethlehem — I mean Epiphanius, the great high priest, the wall of the Cypriots. Since, then, holy Father, because of the multitude of my sins I was not found worthy to see that good place where the precious remains of our holy father the bishop were buried, and the memory of it is with me unceasingly, together with great grief, I therefore entreat your holy paternity to let us know by letter on what day and in what place he was buried. I have sent a man gifted with foresight and found worthy of God's grace — I mean the honorable deacon Callippus — who informed me about your holiness, that you had taken your seat on the throne of the church of Constantia. For while I was weeping and lamenting over the burial of the holy man, and did not know who had taken the throne, so that I might learn by letter, this same honorable deacon Callippus told me that Sabinus, the abbot of a monastery, had succeeded our father Epiphanius of holy memory. That is why we have sent him over so long and so very difficult a journey by land and sea, so that through your holiness we may obtain what we have asked. Be so kind as to give our warm greetings to your most pure clergy and to all who are under your holiness. Pray for me, holy Father, worthy of the priesthood.
